questions.prompt: What is the Reason field on a change request for?
questions.explanation: It's the project's memory. In six months, when someone asks why a part has a notch in it, the rationale is the only place that answer still exists — the people who knew have graduated.

answers.text: To record why the change was made, for whoever asks in six months
To justify the change to the faculty advisor
To let the system estimate how long the change will take
It's optional paperwork with no downstream use

questions.prompt: How does the CR form flag an item that another assembly uses?
questions.explanation: The item picker shows a where-used warning for selected items. The full impact report (Build readiness) appears once the request is open.

answers.text: It shows a where-used warning on the selected item
It creates a complete impact list automatically
It notifies everyone on the project and lets them self-identify
It scans linked GitHub repositories for matching filenames

questions.prompt: A reviewer rejects your change request. What happens to it?
questions.explanation: The rejected request remains in the record with its review note, if the reviewer entered one.

answers.text: It stays in the record with the review note, if one was entered
It's deleted so the list stays clean
It reopens automatically after a week
It's converted into a task assigned back to you

questions.prompt: What happens when a change request is approved? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Approval releases the selected version and advances the item's revision letter. It records an audit event. It notifies the author and members watching the covered items, but it does not automatically edit BOM links, close tasks, or notify every downstream checkout holder.

answers.text: The selected version is released with a revision letter
An audit event records the approval
The requester is granted XP for the approval
All linked tasks are automatically closed

questions.prompt: Rejecting a change request is a sign the review process has failed.
questions.explanation: False. "Not until after the design review" is a perfectly good outcome, and a team that only ever approves has stopped reviewing. Rejection with a written reason is the process working.

answers.text: True
False

questions.prompt: A required reviewer signed off, then the linked PR received a new commit. What happens before ClubPM can release the revision?
questions.explanation: The sign-off is tied to the proposed Vault versions and PR head. A changed head makes it stale; the reviewer must sign off again after the new PR checks and reviews pass.

answers.text: The reviewer signs off again on the new head after PR checks and review pass
The earlier sign-off remains valid because the CR number is unchanged
GitHub assigns the next Vault revision automatically
Any member can override the stale state

questions.prompt: Build readiness lists a stale assembly warning and a blocker: a component in the BOM has no released revision. What can the admin do?
questions.explanation: Warnings are the reviewer's judgement; blockers stop approval. Release the component first, or add it to this request, and the blocker clears.

answers.text: Release that component (or add it to the request) before approving; the warning alone would not stop approval
Approve now; both findings are advisory
Nothing; stale assemblies always block approval
Approve and let the package build skip the unreleased component

questions.prompt: After a release, someone pushes a newer file to the Vault branch. What happens to that release's package?
questions.explanation: The manifest pins each file by commit and SHA-256. The package is rebuilt only from those pinned bytes; a mismatch fails the build instead of substituting new bytes.

answers.text: Nothing changes; it is built from the pinned commits and hashes, and Verify rebuilds it byte for byte
The package picks up the newer file on its next build
The release is reopened for review automatically
The manifest is regenerated from the current BOM
